Does Invariant Risk Minimization Capture Invariance?

 

Pritish Kamath pritish@ttic.edu          Akilesh Tangella akilesh@ttic.edu          Danica J. Sutherland dsuth@cs.ubc.ca          Nathan Srebro nati@ttic.edu

Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago

Abstract

We show that the Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) formulation of Arjovsky et al. (2019) can fail to capture “natural” invariances, at least when used in its practical “linear” form, and even on very simple problems which directly follow the motivating examples for IRM. This can lead to worse generalization on new environments, even when compared to unconstrained ERM. The issue stems from a significant gap between the linear variant (as in their concrete method IRMv1) and the full non-linear IRM formulation. Additionally, even when capturing the “right” invariances, we show that it is possible for IRM to learn a sub-optimal predictor, due to the loss function not being invariant across environments. The issues arise even when measuring invariance on the population distributions, but are exacerbated by the fact that IRM is extremely fragile to sampling.

1 INTRODUCTION

Machine learning systems tend to seize on spurious correlations present in the training data, and so when presented with out-of-distribution inputs, they can fail spectacularly. For instance, in the spirit of Beery et al. (2018) and Arjovsky et al. (2019), consider a deep neural network trained to classify images as containing a cow or a camel. Suppose that most pictures of cows in the training set are taken in (green) grassy pastures, and those of camels are mostly in (brown) deserts. Then, the neural network is likely to strongly use background color for its predictions – after all, it is a very easy signal to use, and it barely hurts the loss. Such a network, however, will perform poorly at recognizing cows on a beach. How, then, can we design a machine learning system to identify key features of interest – face, shape, body color, etc., of animals – and ignore spurious ones, like the background color?

Standard machine learning algorithms assume a training set independently sampled from a single distribution, and seek good performance only on new samples from the same distribution. There has been much work on models that can adapt to a new distribution given a small number of labeled samples (see e.g. the survey of Redko et al., 2020), or models that are robust to nearby distributions (see e.g. the survey of Rahimian & Mehrotra, 2019). Ideally though, we would hope for a model that can handle even large changes in distribution, without the need for labeled target samples.

In reality, our training data usually does not actually come from a single homogeneous source: we may have collected it from different users, on different continents, in different years. We thus may be able to tell which correlations are stable across environments (and hence are more likely to be the “true” correlations we seek), and which behave differently in different environments (and are more likely to be spurious).

One approach, then, is to attempt to learn an invariant predictor (e.g. Peters et al., 2015; Heinze-Deml et al., 2018; Rojas-Carulla et al., 2018). We might, for instance, assume that for the causally relevant subset SS of the input variables XX, the conditional distribution {Y|XS}\left\{Y|X_{S}\right\} is invariant across data sampled from different environments. This usually requires assuming a meaningful causal graph relating the observed variables. When classifying cows vs. camels based on image pixels, such assumptions are not likely to hold on the input data, though they could potentially apply to the latent variables underlying these images.

The Invariant Risk Minimization (𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}) framework of Arjovsky et al. (2019) tries to find a data representation φ\varphi which discards the spurious correlations, leaving only the “real” signal, by enforcing that the predictor ww acting on that representation is simultaneously optimal in each environment given φ\varphi. For instance, in the cows-vs-camels problem, φ\varphi might remove the background color. Since this gives a challenging bi-level optimization problem, Arjovsky et al. propose a relaxed version, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1}, which assumes ww is a linear predictor. (We will overview the framework in Section 2.) For a thorough overview of how this approach fits into the literature on out-of-domain generalization, see the discussion by Arjovsky et al. and in particular Appendix A of Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz (2021). Subsequent work has provided new approaches for training in the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} paradigm (e.g. Ahuja et al., 2020; Teney et al., 2020) and applications in domains such as interpretable language processing models (Chang et al., 2020).

Despite much initial promise, however, many key questions remain about the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} framework: how well does 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} approximate the exact version of the framework in general settings? Do invariant predictors always generalize well on unseen environments? When does a set of training environments allow us to find representations invariant across a broader set of target environments? How does the framework and/or the algorithm behave on finite samples?

Our Contributions

We advance the understanding of several core questions about the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} framework.

In Section 3, we study a simple setting of environments over 𝒳={0,1}2\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}^{2}, abstracting the Colored-MNIST problem studied by Arjovsky et al. (2019). We show that sometimes 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} with linear ww can provably fail to find a “truly” invariant predictor, even when solved with respect to the population loss, and even if we provide infinitely many training environments. In fact, it finds a predictor that is even worse on out-of-distribution environments than unrestricted 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM}. This issue persists in the 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} implementation.

In Section 4, we note the population loss of even “truly” invariant predictors need not be invariant. We give a simple setting where 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, which minimizes loss over training environments, prefers an invariant predictor with worse out-of-distribution generalization.

In Section 5, we study when it is possible to identify invariant predictors for a broad class of environments on the basis of a small range of training environments. Although this is generally impossible, we show conditions on the environments under which it is possible.

Finally, in Section 6, we point out issues that arise when using the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} paradigm over the distributions of empirical samples rather than the population distributions. Here, even invariant predictors (over the population distributions) might not be invariant when considered over the distribution of empirical samples.

2.1 Notions of Invariance

The 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} paradigm attempts to solve this problem by learning an invariant representation φ:𝒳→𝒵\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z}. For instance, φ\varphi might “throw away” the spurious background color in the cows-vs.-camels example, if e1∈ℰe_{1}\in\mathcal{E} is images from Ireland (where most cow images have grassy backgrounds), and e2∈ℰe_{2}\in\mathcal{E} is from India (with many more images of cows on city streets). The formal definition of invariant is as follows.

Definition 1 (Definition 3 of Arjovsky et al., 2019).

A representation11 1 We always assume φ\varphi and ww are measurable. For further subtleties with Definitions 1 and 3, see Section A.1. φ:𝒳→𝒵\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z} is invariant over a set of environments ℰ\mathcal{E} if there exists a w:𝒵→𝒴^w:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}} such that ww is simultaneously optimal on φ\varphi for all environments e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}, that is, w∈argminw¯:𝒵→𝒴^ℒe(w¯∘φ)w\in\argmin_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi).

This definition is motivated by the following observation of Arjovsky et al. (2019), which corresponds more closely to an intuitive definition of invariance.

Observation 2.

Under Setting A, a representation φ:𝒳→𝒵\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z} is invariant over ℰ\mathcal{E} if and only if for all e1,e2∈ℰe_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{E}, it holds that

We give a proof in Section A.2 for completeness.

Crucially, Definition 1 requires that φ\varphi and ww are unrestricted in the space of all (measurable) functions. However, we wish to learn φ\varphi and ww with access to only (finite) training sets SeS_{e} sampled from 𝒟e\mathcal{D}_{e}, for only a small subset of training environments ℰtr⊆ℰ\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{E}. 2.2 Algorithms

Armed with a notion of invariance, we still need a way to pick an invariant predictor based on training environments ℰtr⊆ℰ\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{E}. Arjovsky et al. (2019) proposed the Invariant Risk Minimization objective given by

s.t.∀e∈ℰtr,w∈argminw¯:𝒵→𝒴^ℒe(w¯∘φ),\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}\,\forall e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}},\;w\in\argmin_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi),

which in our notation is equivalent to

minf∈ℐ⁡(ℰtr)∑e∈ℰtrℒe​(f).\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})}\ \ \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(f). (𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM})

Yet, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} remains a bi-level optimization problem. For practical purposes, Arjovsky et al. (2019) proposed to soften this hard constraint, giving the algorithm 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} to approximate 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}:

minφ:𝒳→ℝ∑e∈ℰtrℒe(φ)+λ|∇w|w=1ℒe(w⋅φ)|2.\min_{\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}}\ \ \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\varphi)+\lambda\left|\nabla_{w|w=1}\mathcal{L}_{e}(w\cdot\varphi)\right|^{2}. (𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1})

A natural baseline is the 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} algorithm, which simply minimizes the loss over training environments:

minf:𝒳→𝒴^∑e∈ℰtrℒe(f).\displaystyle\min_{f:\mathcal{X}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\ \ \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(f). (𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM})

While we referred to 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} and 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} as “algorithms” above, there still remain two key details that make these impractical as stated: (i) the loss minimized refers to the population loss, to which we do not have direct access, and (ii) we are assuming that φ\varphi is unrestricted in the space of all functions. Arjovsky et al. (2019) attempt to remedy these issues in 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} by (i) replacing the population loss by the corresponding empirical loss measured over training sets, and (ii) by optimizing φ\varphi over a sufficiently expressive parameterized model, such as a deep neural network, using gradient-based local search methods.

Nevertheless, as we discuss shortly, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} does not capture 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} even when operating on the population loss with unrestricted φ\varphi. Unless otherwise stated, we always consider 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} and 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} as operating over population losses.

2.3 Related Work

Rosenfeld et al. (2021) demonstrate an example where there exists a near-optimal solution to the 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} objective, that nearly matches performance of 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} on training environments, but does no better than 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} on environments that are “far” away from the training distributions. This example relies on environments which barely overlap, allowing the representation to simply “memorize” the training environments. Indeed, Ahuja et al. (2021) argue that 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} can have an advantage over 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} only when the support of the different environment distributions have a significant overlap. Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz (2021) find empirically that with current models and data augmentation techniques, 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} achieves state-of-the-art practical performance in domain generalization. Nagarajan et al. (2021), meanwhile, theoretically study the behavior of 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} for domain generalization.

Note that in prior work, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}/𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} and 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} are often referred to interchangeably. As we demonstrate, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} can behave very differently from 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, even on simple examples that motivated the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} approach.

3 COLORED-MNIST AND TWO-BIT ENVIRONMENTS

To illustrate the utility of the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} approach and 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} in particular, Arjovsky et al. (2019) introduced the Colored-MNIST problem, a synthetic task derived from MNIST (LeCun et al., 2010). While MNIST images are grayscale, in Colored-MNIST each image is colored either red or green in a way that correlates strongly (but spuriously) with the class label. Here 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} learns to exploit the color, and fails at test time when the direction of correlation with the color is reversed.

To understand the behavior of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} on Colored-MNIST, we study an abstract version based on two bits of input, where YY is the binary label to be predicted, X1X_{1} corresponds to the label of the handwritten digit (0-4 or 5-9), and X2X_{2} corresponds to the color (red or green). We represent each environment ee with two parameters αe,βe∈[0,1]\alpha_{e},\beta_{e}\in[0,1]. The distribution 𝒟e\mathcal{D}_{e} is defined as

X1\displaystyle X_{1} ←Y⋅Rad⁡(αe),\displaystyle\penalty\ \leftarrow\penalty\ Y\cdot\mathrm{Rad}(\alpha_{e}), (Two-Bit-Envs)
X2\displaystyle X_{2} ←Y⋅Rad⁡(βe),\displaystyle\penalty\ \leftarrow\penalty\ Y\cdot\mathrm{Rad}(\beta_{e}),

where Rad⁡(δ)\mathrm{Rad}(\delta) is a random variable taking value −1-1 with probability δ\delta and +1+1 with probability 1−δ1-\delta. For convenience, we denote an environment ee as (αe,βe)(\alpha_{e},\beta_{e}).

Following the experiments with Colored-MNIST as done by Arjovsky et al. (2019), we consider a set of environments ℰα≔{(α,βe):0<βe<1}\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}\coloneqq\left\{(\alpha,\beta_{e}):0<\beta_{e}<1\right\}. It can be shown that there only two predictors in ℐ⁡(ℰα)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}), one being the trivial 00-predictor, and another that depends only on X1X_{1} (see proof of Proposition 5 for details).

But, if we evaluate the ability of these predictors to generalize far out of distribution to a case where the (spurious) correlation of X2X_{2} has flipped entirely, e=(0.25,0.9)e=(0.25,0.9), f𝖤𝖱𝖬f_{\mathsf{ERM}} will give the wrong (binary) prediction 90% of the time, and get square loss ℒe​(f𝖤𝖱𝖬)=0.985\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{\mathsf{ERM}})=0.985. It is even worse than the trivial 00-predictor, ℒe​(f0)=0.5\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{0})=0.5.

It turns out that 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} also learns the predictor f𝖨𝖱𝖬f_{\mathsf{IRM}} here, demonstrating the utility of this relaxation of 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}. This raises a natural question:

Does 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} always learn the same predictor as 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}?

Arjovsky et al. (2019, Section 4.1) considered a specialized linear family of environments, where they proved that indeed 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} learns an invariant predictor, as learned by 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, for any ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} with a sufficient number of environments in ‘‘general position.’’33 3 The problem (Two-Bit-Envs) does not fit the setting of their Theorem 9, because flipping signs cannot be phrased as independent additive noise. (See also Rosenfeld et al., 2021, Section 5.) It was left to future work whether 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} learns invariant predictors in the sense of 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} more generally as well.

A failure mode of 𝗜𝗥𝗠𝓢\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝗜𝗥𝗠𝘃𝟭\mathsf{IRMv1}

We show that in fact for a simple set of two-bit environments, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} finds a predictor worse than that learned by 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, and even worse than the one learned by 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM}.

This occurs, e.g., for ℰ=ℰ0.1\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{0.1} with training environments ℰtr={e1=(0.1,0.2),e2=(0.1,0.25)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\left\{e_{1}=(0.1,0.2),e_{2}=(0.1,0.25)\right\}. The learned predictors are (approximately) as follows.

The relation between 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} and 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} is as expected: 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} trades slightly worse loss on the training environments for much better extrapolation to the distant environment etest=(0.1,0.9)∈ℰ0.1e_{\mathrm{test}}=(0.1,0.9)\in\mathcal{E}_{0.1}. But while 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} also suffers slightly on the training environments, it is even worse than 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} at extrapolation to eteste_{\mathrm{test}}! The invariant feature X1X_{1} is more correlated with YY than the non-invariant feature X2X_{2} in all of the training environments, and yet 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} depends on X2X_{2} even more seriously than 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} does.

Moreover, this is not a carefully-selected pathological example that would go away with more training environments. In fact, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} chooses the same predictor even if we include any number of additional training environments (0.1,βe)(0.1,\beta_{e}) for βe<0.28\beta_{e}<0.28. Indeed, we show that for these two-bit environments ℰα\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}, any two training environments are sufficient to recover the set of all invariant predictors (proof in Appendix B).

Proposition 5.

Under Setting A, for all α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and ℰtr={e1,e2}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\left\{e_{1},e_{2}\right\} for any two distinct e1,e2∈ℰαe_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{E}_{\alpha},

(i) ​ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)=ℐ𝒮​(ℰα) and (ii) ​ℐ​(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰα).\text{(i) }\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha})\quad\text{ and }\quad\text{(ii) }\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}).

Thus, the issue is not just that we have don’t have enough training environments. Rather, as we will now show, what 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} determines to be an “invariant predictor” is broader than our intuitive sense – or 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}’s notion – of what it means to be invariant.

In particular, for ℰ0.1\mathcal{E}_{0.1} with ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}}, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}’s feasible set of solutions is ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)⊋ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})\supsetneq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}), or equivalently ℐ𝒮​(ℰ0.1)⊋ℐ⁡(ℰ0.1)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{0.1})\supsetneq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{0.1}).

If the average value of βe\beta_{e} exceeds 0.720.72, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} switches to the other solution f2f_{2}.

Figure 3 shows55 5 The 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} objective can be non-convex, even for ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}}, and typical optimization algorithms sometimes find local minima. We instead solved 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} by explicitly enumerating the (odd) stationary points. the solution smoothly interpolating between f𝖤𝖱𝖬f_{\mathsf{ERM}} and f𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮f_{\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}}, with the reliance on X2X_{2} increasing as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty.

ℓ𝐥𝐨𝐠\ell_{\mathrm{log}} loss

A similar failure mode occurs for ℓlog\ell_{\mathrm{log}} on ℰ0.05\mathcal{E}_{0.05} when training on ℰtr={(0.05,0.1),(0.05,0.2)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\{(0.05,0.1),(0.05,0.2)\}. We give more details in Section B.2.

3.1 Experiments with Colored-MNIST

We now confirm that the failure mode studied above can also arise in practical training of deep networks based on 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1}. Colored-MNIST corresponds to the two-bit environments above, where X1X_{1} is a (grayscale) image from MNIST, and X2X_{2} is a color (red or green) which is assigned to that image.66 6 In practice, we sample the image X1X_{1} first and then flip YY with probability αe\alpha_{e}; this is equivalent. Thus, a learning algorithm which finds global minima of the 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} population-level objective in a model capable of perfectly classifying MNIST digits would behave exactly as described above. In practice, however, we optimize empirical estimates of the risk and gradient penalty, in a model class which may not contain an exactly perfect digit classifier, with an algorithm which may not find the global optimum.

One significant practical issue with 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} is in hyperparameter tuning, since we wish to find models which generalize to environments quite different from ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}. Arjovsky et al. (2019) chose hyperparameters arbitrarily for their 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} networks, and for 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} by selecting a network with randomly selected hyperparameters which performed the best on the test set (specifically, the model with the highest minimum accuracy on ℰtr∪{etest}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\cup\{e_{\mathrm{test}}\}). Since this significantly advantages 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} over 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM}, we instead consider the distribution of performances with random hyperparameters from the same proposal distribution as used by Arjovsky et al.. We also note which of these models minimized the objective on ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} (using a fixed, large λ\lambda to compare the objective for 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1}). Currently, there is no known principled approach for choosing λ\lambda; as noted by Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz (2021), this is often critical to the practical performance of 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}.

Arjovsky et al. (2019) use a fully-connected ReLU network with one hidden layer, operating on the red and green channels of a 14×1414\times 14 image. Running 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} and 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} on this architecture with ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}} in the original Colored-MNIST problem shows (Figure 4(a)) that 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} handily outperforms 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} in test loss, though it does not quite achieve the performance of the best possible f𝖨𝖱𝖬f_{\mathsf{IRM}}, and model selection based on ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} would choose a predictor notably worse on the test set than the null predictor f0f_{0}. Moving to the example failure mode discussed above, this is no longer the case (Figure 4(b)): the two algorithms perform about the same in test loss, with model selection on ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} selecting a model with performance about the same as f0f_{0} for each algorithm. Although the practical instantiation of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} clearly suffers here, it is not worse than 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} as we would expect for the population-optimal solutions.

In this representation, X1X_{1} (digit) and X2X_{2} (color) are quite “entangled.” In Appendix C, we consider an architecture which processes the grayscale image and total color of the image separately, thus becoming a little closer to the idealized setting (Two-Bit-Envs); here the failure of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} compared to 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM} becomes more apparent. We also explore many variations of the experiment, including experiments with ℓlog\ell_{\mathrm{log}}.

Thus, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}’s surprising failure on the extremely simple problem (Two-Bit-Envs) is essentially reproduced with practical optimization of neural networks on Colored-MNIST.

4 CAN 𝗜𝗥𝗠\mathsf{IRM} FAIL TO CHOOSE THE RIGHT PREDICTOR?

In the previous section, we saw an example where 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} was able to identify ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}), since ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)=ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E})=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}) there, but chose a predictor in ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}) with worse out-of-distribution risk for environments “far from” ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}. This happened because the loss ℒe​(f)\mathcal{L}_{e}(f) of predictors f∈ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)f\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}) need not be the same (invariant) for all environments e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}, and we pick the “wrong” predictor when optimizing ∑e∈ℰtrℒe​(f)\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(f) over f∈ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)f\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}).

Is the same possible for 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, or does its implicit premise that the optimal invariant predictor on ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} will generalize well to ℰ\mathcal{E} hold? 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} can of course fail when ℐ⁡(ℰtr)⊋ℐ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})\supsetneq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}), when the training environments are not diverse enough to identify the right invariances. But what if we do have ℐ⁡(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E})?

The loss of an invariant predictor f∈ℐ⁡(ℰ)f\in\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}) need not be invariant for all e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}: consider e.g. varying amounts of inherent additive noise in a regression setting. This would still be acceptable as long as the best invariant predictor with respect to the population loss is the same for all environments e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}. Contrarily, we now give a simple family of environments ℰ\mathcal{E}, training environments ℰtr⊆ℰ\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{E} satisfying ℐ⁡(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}), and two predictors f1,f2∈ℐ⁡(ℰ)f_{1},f_{2}\in\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}) such that ℒe​(f1)>ℒe​(f2)\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{1})>\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{2}) for all e∈ℰtre\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}, but ℒℰ​(f1)<ℒℰ​(f2)\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{E}}(f_{1})<\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{E}}(f_{2}). Hence 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} prefers f2f_{2} to f1f_{1} based on ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}, but f1f_{1} has better worst-case loss. It is thus generally difficult to handle out-of-distribution prediction in environments with more than one invariant predictor: the invariant predictor which is best on training environments might still perform poorly on unseen test environments, despite being invariant.

Consider environments ℰ\mathcal{E} over 𝒳={−1,0,1}3\mathcal{X}=\left\{-1,0,1\right\}^{3} and 𝒴={−1,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{-1,1\}, where each environment ee is specified by a single parameter θe∈(−1/6,1/3)\theta_{e}\in(-1/6,1/3) as follows:

While the specific form of gθg_{\theta} is a little involved, the main thing to note is that

𝔼𝒟e⁡[gθe​(X1,X2)∣X1]=0=𝔼𝒟e⁡[gθe​(X1,X2)∣X2]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[g_{\theta_{e}}(X_{1},X_{2})\mid X_{1}]=0=\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[g_{\theta_{e}}(X_{1},X_{2})\mid X_{2}]\,

which means that 𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y|X1]=0.3​X1\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y|X_{1}]=0.3X_{1} as well as 𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y|X2]=0.3​X2\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y|X_{2}]=0.3X_{2}. Thus for ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}}, ℐ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}) contains the predictors f1​(x)=0.3​x1f_{1}(x)=0.3\,x_{1} and f2​(x)=0.3​x2f_{2}(x)=0.3\,x_{2}. In fact, as shown in Appendix D, 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} will indeed pick among these predictors in ℐ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}) for almost all ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} containing at least two distinct environments:

Proposition 6.

In Setting A, for ℰ\mathcal{E} as above, it holds for Lebesgue-almost all ℰtr⊆ℰ\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{E} with |ℰtr|≥2|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}|\geq 2 that ℐ⁡(ℰ)=ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}). Moreover, any f∈ℐ⁡(ℰ)f\in\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}) depends on at most one of x1x_{1} or x2x_{2}.

Focusing on the case of ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}}, the loss of the predictors can be seen to be77 7 This calculation does not need the specific form of gθg_{\theta}., for any e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E},

ℒe​(f1)=0.47 and ℒe​(f2)=0.47+0.09⋅θe\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{1})=0.47\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{2})=0.47+0.09\cdot\theta_{e}

Thus, if ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} only contains environments ee corresponding to θe<0\theta_{e}<0, we will have that ℒe​(f2)<ℒe​(f1)\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{2})<\mathcal{L}_{e}(f_{1}) for all e∈ℰtre\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}, and yet the invariant predictor that minimizes supe∈ℰℒe​(⋅)\sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\cdot) is f1f_{1}. See Figure 12 (Appendix D) for an illustration of these loss as a function of θe\theta_{e}.

𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}’s notion of invariance ensures 𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z] is invariant across ℰ\mathcal{E}, but allows the loss of the corresponding predictor ℒe​(f)\mathcal{L}_{e}(f) to differ across e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}. Here, in fact the full conditional distribution {Y∣φ⁡(X)=z}\left\{Y\mid\varphi(X)=z\right\} is also invariant across ℰ\mathcal{E}, but even so, the loss varies. If we enforced a stronger notion of invariance which requires the entire joint distribution {(Y,φ⁡(X))}(X,Y)∼𝒟e\left\{(Y,\varphi(X))\right\}_{(X,Y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{e}} to be invariant across all e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}, we would not have faced this issue, since ℒe\mathcal{L}_{e} would then be invariant, and indeed would pick f1f_{1} in the example above. Yet this joint invariance is clearly too strict for some problems: it is impossible to achieve if the marginal distribution of YY differs across environments, and it is easy to construct other ℰ\mathcal{E} where 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} allows the intuitively-correct predictor but joint invariance allows only a trivial constant predictor.

Thus, 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} is not always guaranteed to achieve optimal out-of-distribution loss, even when all the right invariances are captured by the training environments. The “right” notion of invariance really depends on what we know about the set of all environments ℰ\mathcal{E}.

5 WHEN DOES INVARIANCE GENERALIZE?

In the examples of Sections 3 and 4, it held that 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} or 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} were able to identify predictors invariant over all, even unseen, environments: specifically, ℐ𝒲​(ℰ)=ℐ𝒲​(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{E})=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}). That this holds is an implicit premise of the 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} framework. Yet it is unclear in general when invariances discovered on training environments will generalize to unseen environments. We now give some partial answers to this question.

For an arbitrary ℰ\mathcal{E}, we of course cannot expect invariances observed across ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} to generalize over ℰ\mathcal{E}: simply consider adding a single entirely “irrelevant” ee to ℰ\mathcal{E}. To provide some structure, we consider parameterized sets of environments ℰ\mathcal{E}. For simplicity, we focus on finite 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, with 𝒴⊆ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}. Let Δ𝒳×𝒴\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} denote the space of all probability distributions over 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, and let Θ⊆ℝd\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. A map Π:Θ→Δ𝒳×𝒴\Pi:\Theta\to\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} naturally defines a set of environments ℰΠ\mathcal{E}_{\Pi} corresponding to the set of distributions {Π⁡(θ):θ∈Θ}\left\{\Pi(\theta):\theta\in\Theta\right\}. For example, the two-bit environments ℰα\mathcal{E}_{\alpha} of Section 3 are parameterized by the map Π:θ↦e=(α,θ)\Pi:\theta\mapsto e=(\alpha,\theta), for θ∈Θ=(0,1)\theta\in\Theta=(0,1).

For Θtr⊆Θ\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\Theta and ℰtr={Π⁡(θ)∣θ∈Θtr}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\left\{\Pi(\theta)\mid\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}\right\},
when does it hold that ℐ⁡(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi})?

Note that ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)⊆ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi})\subseteq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}) always holds, but for any hope of ℐ⁡(ℰtr)⊆ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})\subseteq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}), we must assume ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} contains a “representative set” of environments from ℰΠ\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}.

The most basic assumption to begin with is simply that Π\Pi is continuous. This is insufficient to guarantee invariance, even for very large Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}: the map might simply “change directions” outside of ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}. We give a simple example below (proof in Appendix E), where even an uncountable number of environments in ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} do not allow us to understand the full behavior of ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Proposition 7.

There exists a continuous map Π:(0,1)→Δ𝒳×𝒴\Pi:(0,1)\to\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} such that for Θtr=(0,14)\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}=\left(0,\frac{1}{4}\right) and ℰtr=Π⁡(Θtr)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\Pi(\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}), it holds that ℐ⁡(ℰtr)≠ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})\neq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}).

On the other hand, if Π\Pi is not only continuous but also analytic, we can guarantee, under some conditions, that invariances over ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} continue to hold over all of ℰΠ\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}. Let Π(x,y)​(θ):=Pr(X,Y)∼Π⁡(θ)⁡[X=x,Y=y]\Pi_{(x,y)}(\theta):=\Pr_{(X,Y)\sim\Pi(\theta)}[X=x,Y=y] for each (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}. We say the map Π:Θ→Δ𝒳×𝒴\Pi:\Theta\to\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} is analytic if, for each (x,y)∈𝒳×𝒴(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, Π(x,y):Θ→[0,1]\Pi_{(x,y)}:\Theta\to[0,1] is analytic in θ\theta.

Proposition 8.

Let Θtr⊆Θ⊆ℝd\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, where Θ\Theta is a connected, open set. Suppose Π:Θ→Δ𝒳×𝒴\Pi:\Theta\to\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} is analytic, 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} are finite and ℰtr=Π⁡(Θtr)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\Pi(\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}). Then, under Setting A,

  1. (i)

    For almost all Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}} with |Θtr|≥2|\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}|\geq 2: ℐ⁡(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}).

  2. (ii)

    For all Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}} with non-zero Lebesgue measure: ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)=ℐ𝒮​(ℰΠ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}).

The key step is that when Π\Pi is analytic, the conditional expectations 𝔼Π⁡(θ)⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]\Ex_{\Pi(\theta)}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z] and the gradient ∇w|w=1ℒΠ⁡(θ)​(w⋅φ)\nabla_{w|w=1}\mathcal{L}_{\Pi(\theta)}(w\cdot\varphi) are analytic functions in θ\theta; the result is far stronger, however, for ℐ\mathcal{I} (where the set of representations is finite) than for ℐ𝒮\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}, where our analysis requires uncountably many training environments. A version of Proposition 8 holds even for infinite spaces 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴⊆ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, under a technical definition of analyticity of Π\Pi (details in Appendix E), although in this case our result for ℐ\mathcal{I} also requires ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} to have positive measure.

Recall that the examples studied in Sections 3 and 4 indeed had analytic parameterizations, and hence Proposition 8 implies that ℐ⁡(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}) holds for (almost) all ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} with at least two distinct environments.

6 IRM WITH FINITE SAMPLES

Except for Section 3.1, we have so far only discussed algorithms (𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}, and 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1}) defined in terms of the population losses of training environments. In practice, however, we need to work with a finite number of samples from each training environment. If we directly apply 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} or 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} as stated in ( IRM ) to empirical distributions, all correlations will have a small amount of noise, and it is extremely likely that the set of invariant predictors becomes empty.

On the other hand, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} for a fixed λ\lambda could be robust to sampling. We illustrate this in the two-bit environments of Section 3. Consider training environments ℰtr={(0.25,0.1),(0.25,0.2),(0.25,0.3)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\left\{(0.25,0.1),(0.25,0.2),(0.25,0.3)\right\}: both 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} and 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} are able to learn an invariant predictor. However, when sampling finite datasets, we only have that the empirical distribution of the two environments will be close to – but not exactly the same as – the true distribution; there may not be any exactly-invariant predictors. We illustrate this by evaluating 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} on a set of training environments ℰtr′={(0.245,0.105),(0.255,0.195),(0.251,0.302)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}^{\prime}=\left\{(0.245,0.105),(0.255,0.195),(0.251,0.302)\right\}, as a proxy for empirical distributions we see from finite samples. 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} learns the trivial 00 predictor f0f_{0}; Figure 5 shows the behavior of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} for increasing λ\lambda.

For a fixed empirical distribution, it is likely that as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} approaches 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}, and does not find a good invariant predictor. If we instead take n→∞n\to\infty for a fixed λ\lambda, though, we should approach the population version of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1}, and hence taking λ→∞\lambda\to\infty at an appropriate rate as n→∞n\to\infty may approach the population 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} predictor. Ahuja et al. (2021) recently considered a variant of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} where the constraints ( ∇ w ) defining ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}) need to hold ε\varepsilon-approximately. When training on the objective with finite samples, they bounds the sample complexity to get an out-of-distribution loss close to that of the corresponding population version of this ε\varepsilon-𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}.

Given the discrepancy between 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} as pointed out in Section 3, however, it is important to make 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} itself more robust to finite samples. For instance, one possible approach would be to relax the requirement of w∈argminw¯:𝒵→𝒴^ℒe(w¯∘φ)w\in\argmin_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi) to

ℒe(w∘φ)≤minw¯:𝒵→𝒴^ℒe(w¯∘φ)+ε\mathcal{L}_{e}(w\circ\varphi)\penalty\ \leq\penalty\ \min_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\ \mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi)+\varepsilon

for a suitable ε>0\varepsilon>0. How to practically implement a version of this ε\varepsilon-𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} remains an open challenge.

7 DISCUSSION

The 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} framework of Arjovsky et al. (2019) proposes a promising new paradigm of learning, which attempts to exploit information we usually ignore to find models robust to even some quite dramatic changes in the input distribution. We have helped shed light on the applicability of this framework.

We now know that 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} can be surprisingly different from 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, even on very simple environments. This emphasizes the importance of finding practical algorithms to approximate 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒲\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{W}} for some nonlinear class of functions 𝒲\mathcal{W}.

We also know that even for 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM}, choosing among invariant predictors can also be vital for out-of-domain generalization, and there exist cases where these algorithms choose the wrong one for out-of-distribution robustness. This holds even if we insist on a stronger notion of invariance, namely that of the conditional distribution {Y∣φ⁡(X)}(X,Y)∼𝒟e\left\{Y\mid\varphi(X)\right\}_{(X,Y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{e}}. To truly handle worst-case out-of-distribution generalization, a stronger notion is needed: for example, it suffices to require invariance of the joint distribution {(Y,φ⁡(X))}(X,Y)∼𝒟e\left\{(Y,\varphi(X))\right\}_{(X,Y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{e}}, but this seems overly stringent.

We also now know more about the possibility of generalizing invariances learned from ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} to a larger set of environments ℰ\mathcal{E}. With significant structure on ℰ\mathcal{E}, it is possible to ensure ℐ⁡(ℰ)=ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}), but substantial questions remain as to the situation for ℐ𝒮\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}} or more realistic assumptions on ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Finally, we demonstrated that 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} and even 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} can be surprisingly brittle when run on samples, rather than populations. Thus more analysis, and perhaps new algorithms, are needed to realize the promise of this framework in practice.

Appendix A More details on Section 2

A.1 Subtleties involving Definitions 1 and 3

Definition 1 implicitly assumes that a minimizer w∈argminw¯:𝒵→𝒴^ℒe(w¯∘φ)w\in\argmin_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi) exists. This may not always be the case: for example, if we take logistic loss, there will be no exact maximizer if the problem under φ\varphi is separable, i.e. {Y∣φ⁡(X)=z}\left\{Y\mid\varphi(X)=z\right\} is constant for each z∈𝒵φez\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e}. To handle such cases, Definition 1 can be modified as follows.

Definition 9.

A representation φ:𝒳→𝒵\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z} is invariant for a set of environments ℰ\mathcal{E} if for all ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a w:𝒵→𝒴^w:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}} such that ww is simultaneously ε\varepsilon-optimal on φ\varphi for all environments e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}: that is, we have that ℒe(w∘φ)≤infw¯:𝒵→𝒴^ℒe(w¯∘φ)+ε\mathcal{L}_{e}(w\circ\varphi)\leq\inf_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi)+\varepsilon.

A related problem arises in Definition 3, where ℒe​(w¯∘φ)\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi) may not have a minimizer inside 𝒲\mathcal{W}. In addition to the case where the data is separable (and hence we would want ww to take values ±∞\pm\infty), a similar problem can arise even for square loss if 𝒲\mathcal{W} contains points arbitrarily close to the conditional expectation function but not the conditional expectation function itself; this can happen, for instance, if 𝒲\mathcal{W} is a Gaussian RKHS and the conditional expectation is L2L_{2}-integrable but not in the RKHS. To work around this problem, we can allow ww to lie in an appropriate “closure” of 𝒲\mathcal{W}.

A.2 Proofs of 2 and 4

The following observation was made by Arjovsky et al. (2019). We include a proof, for completeness and clarity.

See 2

Proof.

Suppose the representation φ:𝒳→𝒵\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Z} is invariant for ℰ\mathcal{E}. That is, there exists a predictor w:𝒵→ℝw:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} such that w∈argminw¯:𝒵→ℝℒe(w¯∘φ)w\in\argmin_{\overline{w}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi) simultaneously for all environments e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}. In other words, for all e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E} and z∈𝒵φez\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e}, it holds that w⁡(z)∈argminω∈ℝ⁡𝔼𝒟e⁡[ℓ⁡(ω,Y)∣φ⁡(X)=z]w(z)\in\argmin_{\omega\in\mathbb{R}}\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}\left[\ell(\omega,Y)\mid\varphi(X)=z\right].

First, consider the case of ℓ=ℓsq\ell=\ell_{\mathrm{sq}}. It follows that w⁡(z)=𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]w(z)=\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}\left[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z\right] for all e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E} and z∈𝒵φez\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e}. In particular, it holds for all e1,e2∈ℰe_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{E} and z∈𝒵φe1∩𝒵φe2z\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e_{1}}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e_{2}} that 𝔼𝒟e1⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]=𝔼𝒟e2⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]=w⁡(z)\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e_{1}}}\left[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z\right]=\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e_{2}}}\left[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z\right]=w(z).

Conversely, suppose that φ\varphi is such that 𝔼𝒟e1⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]=𝔼𝒟e2⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e_{1}}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z]=\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e_{2}}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z] for all z∈𝒵φe1∩𝒵φe2z\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e_{1}}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e_{2}} and all e1,e2∈ℰe_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{E}. Then, w⁡(z)≔𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]w(z)\coloneqq\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z] for any ee such that z∈𝒵φez\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e} is well-defined and gives a predictor ww that is simultaneously optimal for all environments.

The case of ℓlog\ell_{\mathrm{log}} is handled similarly by noting that the minimizer of 𝔼𝒟e⁡[ℓlog​(ω,Y)∣φ⁡(X)=z]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}\left[\ell_{\mathrm{log}}(\omega,Y)\mid\varphi(X)=z\right], given by

ω=log⁡(Pr𝒟e⁡[Y=1∣φ⁡(X)=z]Pr𝒟e⁡[Y=−1∣φ⁡(X)=z])=log⁡(1+𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]1−𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]),\omega\penalty\ =\penalty\ \log\left(\frac{\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y=1\mid\varphi(X)=z]}{\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y=-1\mid\varphi(X)=z]}\right)\penalty\ =\penalty\ \log\left(\frac{1+\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z]}{1-\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z]}\right)\,,

uniquely corresponds to 𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z]. ∎

The following lemma is implicit in Arjovsky et al., 2019. See 4

Proof.

We prove the lemma in the following three parts.

𝓘​(𝓔)⊆𝓘𝓢​(𝓔)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E})\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}).

Thus, we have w′∘φ′=w∘φ=fw^{\prime}\circ\varphi^{\prime}=w\circ\varphi=f. (Suppose for contradiction that this is not the case. Thus, we get f∈ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)f\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}).

𝓘𝓦𝐥𝐢𝐧𝒅​(𝓔)⊆𝓘𝓢​(𝓔)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{lin}}^{d}}(\mathcal{E})\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}).

The proof of the above part shows, more generally, that ℐ𝒲​(ℰ)⊆ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{E})\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}) for any 𝒲\mathcal{W} that is closed under scalar multiplications (that is, w∈𝒲⟹c⋅w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}\implies c\cdot w\in\mathcal{W} for all c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}), it holds that ℐ𝒲​(ℰ)⊆ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathcal{E})\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}). Given f∈ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)f\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}), let φ:𝒳→ℝ\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} and w:ℝ→ℝw:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be such that f=w∘φf=w\circ\varphi, where w∈argminw¯∈𝒮⁡ℒe​(w¯∘φ)w\in\argmin_{\overline{w}\in\mathcal{S}}\mathcal{L}_{e}(\overline{w}\circ\varphi) for all e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}. Appendix B More details on Two-Bit Environments (from Section 3)

We show that for all α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), just two environments in ℰα\mathcal{E}_{\alpha} are sufficient to determine both ℐ𝒮​(ℰα)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}) and ℐ⁡(ℰα)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}). Thus, the failure of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} observed in Section 3 is not due to lack of sufficiently representative training environments, but instead due to the difference between what 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} deems an “invariant predictor” and the notion of invariance as in Definition 1.

See 5

Proof.

(i). By definition, we have ℐ𝒮​(ℰα)⊆ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha})\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}), since ℰtr⊆ℰα\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}. We show the converse. As noted in Section 2, for any convex and differentiable loss ℓ\ell and for any set of environments ℰ\mathcal{E} we have that f∈ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)f\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}) if and only if f=1⋅φf=1\cdot\varphi such that ∇w|w=1ℒe​(w⋅φ)=0\nabla_{w|w=1}\mathcal{L}_{e}(w\cdot\varphi)=0 for all e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}. The key observation is that for environment e=(α,βe)e=(\alpha,\beta_{e}),

∇w|w=1ℒe​(w⋅φ)\displaystyle\nabla_{w|w=1}\ \mathcal{L}_{e}(w\cdot\varphi) ≔∑x1,x2,yPr𝒟e⁡[X1=x1,X2=x2,Y=y]⋅∇w|w=1ℓ​(w⋅φ⁡(x1,x2),y)\displaystyle\penalty\ \coloneqq\penalty\ \sum_{x_{1},x_{2},y}\ {\textstyle\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}}[X_{1}=x_{1},X_{2}=x_{2},Y=y]\cdot\nabla_{w|w=1}\ell(w\cdot\varphi(x_{1},x_{2}),y)
=∑x1,x2,y((1−α)​𝟙x1=y+α​𝟙x1≠y)⋅((1−βe)​𝟙x2=y+βe​𝟙x2≠y)⋅∇w|w=1ℓ​(w⋅φ⁡(x1,x2),y)\displaystyle\penalty\ =\penalty\ \sum_{x_{1},x_{2},y}\ ((1-\alpha)\mathds{1}_{x_{1}=y}+\alpha\mathds{1}_{x_{1}\neq y})\cdot((1-\beta_{e})\mathds{1}_{x_{2}=y}+\beta_{e}\mathds{1}_{x_{2}\neq y})\cdot\nabla_{w|w=1}\ell(w\cdot\varphi(x_{1},x_{2}),y)

is affine in βe\beta_{e}. In particular, it can be decomposed as ∇w|w=1ℒe​(w⋅φ)=F⁡(φ)+βe​G​(φ)\nabla_{w|w=1}\ \mathcal{L}_{e}(w\cdot\varphi)=F(\varphi)+\beta_{e}G(\varphi) for some functions FF and GG. This implies F⁡(φ)+βe​G​(φ)=0F(\varphi)+\beta_{e}G(\varphi)=0 for all βe∈(0,1)\beta_{e}\in(0,1), and hence f∈ℰαf\in\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}.

(ii). By definition, we have that ℐ⁡(ℰα)⊆ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha})\subseteq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}), since ℰtr⊆ℰα\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}. We show the converse by establishing that the only invariant predictors in ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}) are those that do not depend on X2X_{2}. By Observation 2, we have that φ\varphi is invariant over ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} if and only if 𝔼𝒟e1⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]=𝔼𝒟e2⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e_{1}}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z]=\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e_{2}}}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z] for all z∈𝒵φe1∩𝒵φe2z\in\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e_{1}}\cap\mathcal{Z}_{\varphi}^{e_{2}}. In other words, φ\varphi is invariant over ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} if and only if 𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣(X1,X2)∈φ−1​(z)]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid(X_{1},X_{2})\in\varphi^{-1}(z)] is identical for e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} as long as Pr𝒟e[φ(X1,X2)=z]\Pr_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[\varphi(X_{1},X_{2})=z] is non-zero in both environments.

In Table 1, we compute 𝔼𝒟e⁡[Y∣(X1,X2)∈S]\Ex_{\mathcal{D}_{e}}[Y\mid(X_{1},X_{2})\in S] for all possible non-empty subsets S⊆{−1,1}2S\subseteq\{-1,1\}^{2}, in terms of the environment parameters α\alpha and βe\beta_{e} and track which of these depend or do not depend on βe\beta_{e}. The ones that depend on βe\beta_{e} can be seen to be distinct for any two distinct values of βe\beta_{e}. Thus, the only invariant representations over ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}} are those corresponding to the following partitions.

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    {{(1,1),(1,−1),(−1,1),(−1,−1)}}\left\{\left\{(1,1),(1,-1),(-1,1),(-1,-1)\right\}\right\}, that is, φ⁡(x1,x2)\varphi(x_{1},x_{2}) is constant. B.2 Case of logistic loss

We observe a similar phenomenon with logistic loss as was observed for square loss. Figure 7 shows the population square losses ℒe\mathcal{L}_{e} for each of the predictors in ℐ𝒮​(ℰ0.05)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{0.05}) for all e∈ℰ0.05e\in\mathcal{E}_{0.05}. Thus, no matter how many training environments are present in ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}, 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}} will choose f1f_{1} as the optimal predictor as long as βe<0.25\beta_{e}<0.25 for all e∈ℰtre\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}. On the other hand, 𝖨𝖱𝖬\mathsf{IRM} with just two environments learns the predictor f𝖨𝖱𝖬f_{\mathsf{IRM}}.

We also note that the value α=0.05\alpha=0.05 is not special; a similar phenomenon as above is observed in ℰα\mathcal{E}_{\alpha} for any value of α<0.077\alpha<0.077.

Appendix C More Colored-MNIST experiments

We now consider more details and variations of the Colored-MNIST experiments of Section 3.1.

The architecture used by Arjovsky et al. (2019) is fully connected, mapping inputs of dimension 2⋅14⋅142\cdot 14\cdot 14 to hidden dimension hh, from hh to hh, and then from hh to a scalar prediction, with ReLU activations on each layer except the last. The model is optimized with full-batch Adam for 501 steps, with a scaled penalty on the squared (Frobenius) norm of each parameter, and hyperparameters selected as:

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Hidden dimension hh: ⌊2Uniform[6,9)⌋\lfloor 2^{\mathrm{Uniform}[6,9)}\rfloor.

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Weight of L2L_{2} regularization: 10Uniform[−2,−5)10^{\mathrm{Uniform}[-2,-5)}.

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    Learning rate: 10Uniform[−2.5,−3.5)10^{\mathrm{Uniform}[-2.5,-3.5)}.

  • ▶\blacktriangleright

    For 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1}, the gradient penalty weight λ\lambda is 11 for Uniform​{50,51,…,250}\mathrm{Uniform}\{50,51,\dots,250\} iterations, then 10Uniform[2,6)10^{\mathrm{Uniform}[2,6)}.

In Figure 8, we reproduce the results of Figure 4 (left column) but also show results of versions of the architecture forced to depend only on X1X_{1} or X2X_{2} while training via 𝖤𝖱𝖬\mathsf{ERM}: color-only takes inputs of shape 22, a one-hot indicator for whether the color is red or green, while digit-only receives a flattened grayscale image of dimension 14⋅1414\cdot 14. This allows us to see the amount of variation we can expect based purely on changes in the learning process. We also show (in the right column) a flipped version of the problem, where the invariant feature is color rather than the digit identity; this is the same from the point of view of the abstract Two-Bit environment, but allows us to see how much of the behavior depends on the different way that this network processes digit and color information.

As mentioned in Section 3.1, we also consider a “split” variant of the architecture, which is perhaps closer to the abstract two-bit version. Here, the network has two branches: one takes a grayscale 14×1414\times 14 version of its input, which is processed as in the previous architecture down to a scalar. The other branch takes a one-hot (two-dimensional) indicator for the color, and (via a 2×12\times 1 linear layer) outputs an arbitrary scalar for each color. The top of the network takes in these two scalar values, processes them with an 8-dimensional ReLU layer, then makes a final linear prediction. color-only and digit-only versions simply omit one of those branches. Results for ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}} are shown in Figure 9. Here we most clearly see the “average-case” failure of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝗏𝟣\mathsf{IRMv1} in the color-invariant case.

Similar results for ℓlog\ell_{\mathrm{log}} are shown in Figures 10 and 11. The expected failure mode is generally less visible here, though it is more evident in the color-invariant settings than the digit-invariant ones.

In the supplementary material, we include the PyTorch code, modified from that of Arjovsky et al. (2019), used to produce these results (colored-mnist directory).

We now prove Proposition 8, restated below for convenience. First, we recall a basic fact about analytic functions.

Fact 10 (Mityagin, 2015).

Let Θ\Theta be a connected, open subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The set of zeros {z∈Θ∣g⁡(z)=0}\left\{z\in\Theta\mid g(z)=0\right\} of an analytic function g:Θ→ℝg:\Theta\to\mathbb{R} has non-zero Lebesgue measure in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} if and only if gg is identically 00.

We show how to extend Proposition 8 to the case of infinite (measurable) spaces 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴⊆ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, where |y|≤B|y|\leq B for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} for some known bound BB. Similar to before, let Δ𝒳×𝒴\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} be the set of all probability measures over 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}. For simplicity, we use Ω\Omega to denote 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}.

Definition 11.

For Θ⊆ℝd\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and a measurable space Ω\Omega, the parameterization Π:Θ→ΔΩ\Pi:\Theta\to\Delta_{\Omega} is said to be analytic if for every measurable set S⊆ΩS\subseteq\Omega and every measurable function g:Ω→ℝg:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}, the function

ΠSg​(θ)≔∫ω∈Sg⁡(ω)​𝖽​Πθ​(ω)\Pi^{g}_{S}(\theta)\coloneqq\int_{\omega\in S}g(\omega)\ \mathsf{d}\Pi_{\theta}(\omega)

is an analytic function in θ\theta (where we use Πθ\Pi_{\theta} to denote the measure Π⁡(θ)\Pi(\theta) for simplicity).

We now state the extension of Proposition 8 to the case of infinite (measurable) spaces. In the case of ℐ𝒮​(ℰ)\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}), we will focus on the representations φ:𝒳→ℝ\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} where |φ⁡(x)|≤B|\varphi(x)|\leq B for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. From the point of view of 𝖨𝖱𝖬𝒮\mathsf{IRM}_{\mathcal{S}}, this is without loss of generality because we know that |y|≤B|y|\leq B for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}.

Proposition 12, however, requires a far stronger condition for ℐ⁡(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}): Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}} needs non-zero Lebesgue measure, rather than simply almost all sets of at least two environments as in Proposition 8. The key step in the proof of Proposition 8 that allowed for this stronger statement was that the number of subsets S⊆𝒳S\subseteq\mathcal{X} is finite. We do not know if Proposition 12 can be strengthened to hold for finite Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}; if not, it will be interesting to determine other conditions under which we can get generalization of invariance for finite Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}.

Proposition 12.

Let Θtr⊆Θ⊆ℝd\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}\subseteq\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, where Θ\Theta is a connected, open set and Θtr\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}} has non-zero Lebesgue measure, in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Suppose Π:Θ→Δ𝒳×𝒴\Pi:\Theta\to\Delta_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} is analytic (as in Definition 11), and ℰtr=Π⁡(Θtr)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}=\Pi(\Theta_{\mathrm{tr}}). Then for the ℓsq\ell_{\mathrm{sq}} loss,

(i) ​ℐ​(ℰtr)=ℐ⁡(ℰΠ) and (ii) ​ℐ𝒮​(ℰtr)=ℐ𝒮​(ℰΠ).\text{(i) }\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi})\quad\text{ and }\quad\text{(ii) }\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}})=\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi}).
Proof.

The proof is similar to that of Proposition 8.

Part (i). We have ℐ⁡(ℰΠ)⊆ℐ⁡(ℰtr)\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\Pi})\subseteq\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}) by definition. To show the converse, consider any f=w∘φ∈ℐ⁡(ℰtr)f=w\circ\varphi\in\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}), with φ\varphi invariant over ℰtr\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tr}}. gz​(θ)=𝔼Π⁡(θ)⁡[Y∣φ⁡(X)=z]=∫φ−1​(z)×𝒴y​𝖽​Πθ​(x,y)∫φ−1​(z)×𝒴𝖽​Πθ​(x,y).g_{z}(\theta)\penalty\ =\penalty\ \Ex_{\Pi(\theta)}[Y\mid\varphi(X)=z]\penalty\ =\penalty\ \frac{\int_{\varphi^{-1}(z)\times\mathcal{Y}}\ y\,\mathsf{d}\Pi_{\theta}(x,y)}{\int_{\varphi^{-1}(z)\times\mathcal{Y}}\ \mathsf{d}\Pi_{\theta}(x,y)}.

Let nz​(θ)n_{z}(\theta) and dz​(θ)d_{z}(\theta) denote the numerator and denominator of gz​(θ)g_{z}(\theta), respectively, both of which are analytic in θ\theta by Definition 11 (and boundedness of yy).
